utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution Douglas Stringer, Alex Demirdjian, Thomas Laugel, Marija Bukovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, very briefly. At the end of the day yesterday when you asked us to clarify the witness's answer as to whether she said no, I was told after court she may have said something else. Would it be possible to ask the Registry to provide the parties with the audio- or video-clip at the break so we review that part of her testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will have to inform the parties during the course of the hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Bosanac. May I remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Demirdjian, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I hope you had time to rest last night despite the work we gave you. Did you manage to review the binder we had prepared, including the 19 faxes and documents which were part of your book?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I realise that the Defence didn't get to look at the binder. Would they like to look at it just to ensure that it is accurately reflecting the list of documents we wish to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Doctor, while the Defence is looking through the binder, could you tell us whether you recognise these letters and faxes and notes?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And are these documents which either were sent by you -- or first of all, could you tell us what was in that binder for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That binder contains copies of faxes that I wrote and sent out from Vukovar, and there are notes on my telephone calls and appeals that I communicated by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And these are similar to those that we have seen in the court yesterday?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At this stage if there is no objection, I would like to read on the record the 65 ter numbers of these faxes and notes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: None, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. So the first one at tab 7 is 65 ter 467.13. The second one at tab 8 is 467.14. The next one at tab 9 is 467.16. At tab 10, 467.17. We then have at tab 11, 467.19. At tab 14 we find 467.3. At tab 15 we find 467.5. Tab 10 [sic] we have 65 ter number 482. At tab 24 we have 65 ter 501. At tab 27 we have 65 ter 516. At tab 28 we have 65 ter 518. At tab 30 we have 65 ter 562. At tab 32 we have 65 ter 580. At tab 36 we have 65 ter 602. Then at tab 21 we have 65 ter 486. At tab 25, 65 ter 502. At tab 22 we have 65 ter 490. At tab 17 we have 65 ter 467.7. And at tab 6 we have 65 ter 467.12. Your Honours, our application is to tender all these exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, at line 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- you said tab 10, 65 ter 482. Either the 65 ter number is wrong or the tab number should be 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It is 20, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. So these documents are admitted and marked. Do we get the exhibits numbers now or later, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the documents will be Exhibit P1442 up to and including P1450. I will communicate to the parties the individual exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please continue, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, yesterday you mentioned that you were not the only one sending faxes, and you mentioned particularly that the police station was sending faxes along its line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I would like to show you one or two of these faxes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We would like to display now 65 ter 87.1, please. And in the English version it would be at page 32, and in the B/C/S it's page 20. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you should be able to see a fax dated the 6th of October, 1991. Do you see that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And this seems to be sent from the police station in Vukovar to the police station in Cakovec. Could you just briefly tell us where is Cakovec?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cakovec is a town located in north-west Croatia, and from the Cakovec police station during the aggression on Vukovar, police officers from Cakovec and Varazdin and some other town were deployed in Vukovar. So I suppose this fax was sent to Cakovec for that purpose, to keep them informed on the circumstances under which the policemen from Cakovec were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, on this page, towards the bottom in both the B/C/S and the English version there is a reference to the Eltz castle. Can you tell the Court what exactly is the Eltz castle?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The castle of Eltz Counts is in the centre of Vukovar on the right bank of the Danube, and inside it - before the war and nowadays - is located the museum the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, was there anything in particular in the area of the Eltz castle during the conflict at least at that time, in October 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, in the basement of that Eltz castle the art was placed, taken from the upper floors to the basement, and the archive of the museum was also placed in the basement of that castle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And are you aware of what purpose was the Eltz castle used for during the months of October and November 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never there in that period, so I don't have exact information of the purpose for which that basement was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in the immediate vicinity of the Eltz castle were there any buildings of particular significance?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opposite the castle, below the road, there was a basement; and on the other side of the road in that basement, wine cellars were located from before the Second World War. It was a very solid basement where many civilians found shelter during the aggression on Vukovar and the shelling attacks. I was there looking for places where we could make a safe shelter to house the wounded for whom we had no more room in the hospital. That basement was safe and sturdy, but it had neither electricity nor water so that we, the hospital staff, abandoned the idea of using it as a shelter. However, it was used by many civilians from the surrounding buildings and houses who were looking for a safe place. For the a while the Croatian Radio Vukovar operated from that basement. In the immediate vicinity of that basement there was an atomic shelter where the Defence commander had his headquarters. At the beginning it was Mile Dedakovic, and later it was Branko Borkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in relation to this shelter you were mentioning, during the conflict how safe was it in that shelter?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was rather safe, especially below the road. It was a very good roof. However, the entrance into the basement was often targeted by shelling, and I remember very well on the 15th just before the fall of Vukovar one shell hit the entranceway, killing nine people including one nurse who worked in our physical therapy department, Mrs. Aleksandar, her husband who worked in the post office, their 3-year-old child. Emil walked to the hospital and died there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in terms of the nine people killed on that occasion, can you tell the Court what was their status, as to whether they were civilians or members of the defenders?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were all civilians, but I remember I read something about that incident in a magazine published by the Yugoslav Army that the captain, I think Radic, got a commendation because he managed to hit the entrance into an Ustasha shelter with an artillery shell, and it was actually describing the event, that event in which civilians were killed. I read that piece just after I arrived at the prison in Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page both in the English and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, here we see that a number of people are listed who sought assistance at the medical centre in Vukovar. Could you tell us how this list was compiled?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That list, as I said before -- a police clerk Branko Lukenda was in charge of making a list of the wounded every day, and Tomislav Hegedus, the policeman, was making lists of the dead; and they would send out those reports on a daily basis to their superiors, to the competent institutions in the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you recognise the name at the bottom? I believe it says Chief Zvonimir Rados. I believe in English it's on the third page.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a policeman in that police administration in Vukovar in charge of sending that information to other stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in this bundle there's another fax that I'd like to show you which is on page 1 both in English and in B/C/S. Yes. This time you should be able to see a fax from the 21st of October, 1991. And it appears at this time the police station has sent this fax to the Ministry of Interior in Zagreb. Looking at this list, Dr. Bosanac, it appears again that there is a report about the number of people brought to the hospital. Is this similar to the one we saw just a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I recognise the names of those wounded JNA soldiers, Pavle Teofanovic and Sasa Jovic, and you can see this list also comes from the police, sent to the MUP in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we scroll to the bottom of the page in the B/C/S version, please, and could we go to the next page in the English version. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This one, too, is signed by the same person, Zvonimir Rados; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that this bundle of faxes which is 65 ter 87.1 be admitted. There's 23 pages in B/C/S. All of them are similar in content. You see a list of names of persons who sought assistance at the medical centre, and it is signed by the chief of the police station, and they are dispatched to other police authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So this is a bundle of faxes. How many exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: There are 23 pages, Your Honours. I believe it's one page per fax in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And it's under one 65 ter number?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Under one 65 ter. The originals -- the original 65 ter, 87, has 123 pages. We've made a selection of only 23 pages just for purposes of showing -- or illustrating the point, and these are, yeah, individual pages and under one bundle, as they are all similar in nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But even isn't that a little bit odd to tender that as one document?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, we could -- we could split them; that is not a problem. I just thought because they're of similar nature, it's the same topic pretty much. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If I could briefly state the Defence's position in respect of the bundle. One thing is the list of injured which is provided by individuals related to the MUP who are monitoring what is going on at the hospital, and another thing that's included in this bundle is an extensive description of military activities. I don't believe this witness knows anything about that, can't vouch for it, can't enhance its reliability. Those portions I don't think should be admitted, that's for sure. So I'm not quite sure how the Defence proposes -- or the Prosecution proposes to deal with it. If they want to admit just the two faxes that they've shown to the witness, there would be no objection to that; but as for the remainder, we would object.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Might I make a proposal then, that we put it on the record now, that the purpose for tendering these exhibits is to strictly show that through the police station faxes were sent recording the patients who sought assistance at the medical centre and strictly for that purpose. And, Your Honours, we can perhaps before the second break split those individual faxes into sub-numbers if that could satisfy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: These documents will be admitted for the purpose you indicated, Mr. Demirdjian, after you split them. I think that would be preferable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We'll do that. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, just to be clear. Are we -- do I understand that what has been provisionally admitted are just the two faxes that have been shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, the entire bundle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The entire bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But only for the purpose indicated by Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I would like to move to the end of the -- well, to the fall of Vukovar basically. Could you tell us when you learned about the end of the battle, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke every day to the minister of health, and I was aware that in Zagreb, in a hotel, negotiations were going on about the evacuation of the hospital and the evacuation of civilians from Vukovar. Apart from that, I was present at the police, at the defence headquarters, wherefrom I sent faxes and appeals. So I was aware that very soon there would be an evacuation of all of Vukovar and the defence would fall. I did not know exactly when that would happen. All I knew was that the plan was to begin evacuating the hospital on the 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And around this time were you aware of what the Croatian defenders were doing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me be more clear. You said that you learned about it through -- through the fact that there were negotiations in Zagreb and that there would be an evacuation of the civilian population. Let me put it this way: Did you go to the police station or the defence headquarters around the 17th or the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did go on the 17th November to the defence headquarters, and there I found Marin Vidic, the police chief. They were talking to individual commanders at various defence points. They were discussing evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. The record reflects here that you said "I found Marin Vidic, the police chief." I believe you wanted to enumerate two separate people; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The police chief, who was Stipo Bole, and Marin Vidic; that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the record shows his last name as "Bole"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: P, P-o-l-e. Stipo Pole was the police chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, around this time you told us - you saw earlier yesterday a fax of the 15th of November - that the civilian population started coming to the Vukovar Hospital. What happened on the 17th and 18th of November in relation to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People from the surrounding buildings and houses came to the hospital. I tried to explain to them that there is no room in the hospital, there's no possibility to accommodate them, they should wait to be evacuated in their own homes. But people were afraid because the shooting was still going on, and everybody kept coming to the hospital. We had no food, no water. All we could offer was tea and toast to the children. And we were very busy preparing the wounded for evacuation, preparing the documentation, preparing immobilisation for purposes of transport, putting plaster casts on limbs. We were expecting the International Commission of the Red Cross and European Monitors to come in the morning of the 18th to begin the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you just told us you were expecting the International Commission of the Red Cross and the European Mission to come to the hospital on the morning of the 18th. What led you to believe that this was to be the case?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke overnight with Professor Hebrang by phone, and he said in the morning on Monday at 8.00 there would be two ICRC teams coming to the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, the evacuation itself didn't take place on the 18th; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, who, if anyone, did you speak to on the 18th once you found out the evacuation was not taking place on that day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again I called Minister Hebrang, and I got him on the line. He told me that the ICRC had sent a message that they were indeed in Vukovar and would be at the hospital but that their -- they were currently busy with evacuating civilians in the southern part of town. I again called the European Commission at the I Hotel, and I got some European observers around 9.00 on the line who said that they were in Negoslavci village and that they were unable to arrive as the Yugoslav Army could not guarantee protection and safety, but that they would be arriving as soon as they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on that day, on the 18th of November, was there any agreement between the parties in relation to the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That night between the 17th and the 18th, the agreement was signed in the I Hotel in Zagreb. It was signed by Georges-Marie Chenu, as the representative of the European Mission; then Professor Andrija Hebrang, as the minister on behalf of the Croatian government; and General Andrija Raseta, on behalf of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. If you can give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we have -- could we have 65 ter 601 at tab 35, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, we have a document in front of us. Do you recognise what this is?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the agreement, one of the drafts. I saw one which its heading had a logo of the ICRC. That was a copy of the agreement which I only saw after I was released from prison. I didn't see it before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on this document at item number 1 we see that the parties involved here are the representatives of the Republic of Croatia, the JNA, the ICRC, Medecins sans Frontieres, Maltese Cross. Does that actually reflect your -- the information you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the information I had, which was that evacuation would begin on the 18th of November organised by the ICRC, European observers, the MSF, and the Maltese Order. The idea was that the Maltese Order -- a convoy be organised with their assistance on the Danube in order to evacuate the wounded and civilians. That was the information I had, although I did not believe they would be able to reach Vukovar by the Danube and on a boat, because there was firing nonstop across the Danube from tanks and cannons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at item number 4 in the second part of that paragraph, there is a mention here that both parties will provide suitably equipped and manned ambulances, and we see here numbers of seriously ill and wounded patients. We see the number of 40 here, 40 seriously ill, and remaining 360 or so casualties. Are these numbers an accurate reflection of the number of patients at the hospital on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the figures I notified Professor Hebrang about concerning the type of wounded and ill we had. The 40 were intensive care patients who had been wounded just a few days before that, and the 360 were the rest who were on their beds in the basement, and shelters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, under number 6 we see here that the Republic of Croatia and the JNA will recognise the neutrality of the Vukovar Hospital during a period covering the evacuation and that the hospital will be put under the protection of the ICRC, who will advise both parties of the period of neutrality. Is this something that you were informed about when speaking with Minister Hebrang?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I expected that the ICRC would arrive at the hospital as well as the European observers so that the wounded and sick as well as the staff would be evacuated irrespective of the JNA presence; however, in the next several days it turned out not to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, what did the presence of the EC monitors and the ICRC and the Maltese Cross mean to you at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It meant that the wounded and medical staff would be evacuated in a safe way and that it would offer a kind of protection from the aggressors who had been attempting to destroy us for the past three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, may I ask to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 601 will be Exhibit P1461. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that the evacuation did not take place on the 18th and you were able to speak with Minister Hebrang and a member of the ECMM. What was then said about the evacuation on that day since it had not taken place on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister Hebrang told me that there were daily meetings and that if not on the 18th, they would definitely be there on the 19th, that is to say the ICRC and the European observers. The European observers told me that they would arrive as soon as they were able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, did they arrive at all during the course of the day on the 18th?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on to the 19th of November now, what were you expecting to happen on the morning of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We expected that it would take place on the 19th, but still no one came that morning. Around 9.00 a.m., I managed to get ahold of General Raseta in Zagreb by phone, who told me that evacuation would begin shortly and that Colonel Mile Mrksic was in charge of that area. I asked him where I could find him, and he said that he would find me. Around noon, I received information from people who were in town that the army had entered it and that they were at the bridge. I came to the closest bridge to the hospital, but I did not see any ICRC staff there. I could only see military APCs and reservists as well as different members of paramilitary forces. I asked them where the ICRC was, and one of them told me - and he was their superior on that APCs - that they didn't know anything about it and that it was their task to evacuate people only as far as the bridge and not beyond. It had to do with a part of town --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the name of that part of the town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that I returned to the hospital, and when the first JNA representatives appeared in front of the hospital, I came out, and I asked that the ICRC and ECMM be present. There was a JNA officer who told me that there was no ICRC or ECMM in town and that they were in Negoslavci. I asked that I personally be taken there so that I can get in touch with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just a second, please, Doctor --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before that I asked him --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you. Earlier you were mentioning that -- you asked them where the ICRC was at the bridge and one of them told you who was their superior and that they didn't know anything about it and that it was their task to evacuate people only as far as the bridge and not beyond. And then you mentioned it had to do with a part of town and the interpreters didn't catch the name of that part of town. Could you tell that -- please tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bridge I was at is a railroad bridge spanning the part of the town where the hospital is and Priljevo which is a settlement inside the town itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you were telling us that you asked to be taken to Negoslavci. Did that happen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us how far is Negoslavci from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be precise. Around 7 or 8 kilometres, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And who took you to Negoslavci?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A JNA officer in a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And once you arrived in Negoslavci -- where in Negoslavci did he take you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He took me in front of a family home where there was a sign which said "Staff." I met Colonel Mile Mrksic there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you met Mile Mrksic, how long did your interaction with him last?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe to the Judges what was discussed during this half-hour conversation with Mile Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him about the ICRC and the ECMM. I asked about hospital evacuation. He told me that he was unaware of it all. I told him that General Raseta had signed an agreement on behalf of the JNA. He said that Raseta may well have signed it but that Raseta didn't know what was going on in the field and that only he could decide on evacuation. I told him that the situation at the hospital was very serious, that there were many wounded and that there were wounded soldiers there, that there was no water, that people were out of food and medication and that evacuation should occur as soon as possible. He said that it was possible to evacuate people via Sid and Adasevci, which is a village which is in Serbia next to the Zagreb-Belgrade highway. I insisted that the agreement be honoured and that evacuation should take place along the Bogdanovci-Marinci-Nustar route. It was my information that ambulances awaited there and buses to evacuate the lightly wounded and civilians. He said then that it would only be possible to do that on Wednesday, because they would have to de-mine a part at Zidine. At the time I didn't even know what it meant. It turns out Zidine was a military area near Nustar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, you say here that Mrksic said it would only be possible to do that on Wednesday. Could you perhaps place us --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Now, I understand from what you just told us that he didn't agree with the route. What did he say about the remainder of the items, in relation to the evacuation agreement, which you were informing him about?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Just one moment, Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not sure that the last element has -- depending on how it was translated to the witness, I'm not sure it's accurate to say that she was informing him about the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I can rephrase that. I can rephrase that, because earlier the Doctor did say that she informed Mr. Mrksic of the substance. But let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, earlier you told us that you were informing Mile Mrksic of the existence of the evacuation [sic]. You told us you were expecting the ECMM and the ICRC to be present. You've now told us he didn't agree with the route to be taken. What was said, if anything, about the other aspects of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that the ICRC and ECMM would shortly arrive at the hospital. I told him we were expecting them as it was contained in the agreement. Then the driver returned me to the hospital. In the village, at the end of the road I saw a vehicle of the ECMM, and I asked the driver to take me there to get in touch with them. However, he said he would need to ask for permission to do so, and he went inside the staff building. When he returned, he said he was ordered to take me back to the hospital. So I wasn't able to establish contact that day with the ECMM or the ICRC in Negoslavci. I was returned back to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, on your way back --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, at line 7 of page 19, you asked: Doctor, earlier you tell us that you were informing Mile Mrksic about the existence of the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I think you meant agreement, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The agreement. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, on your way back to the hospital, did anything in particular happen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was important for me. En route back to the hospital I met my mother who was moving on foot with a group of people around town. She could barely walk. She was dragging her headscarf in the dust, and I asked that she be picked up with -- by car and -- actually, to be taken in the car that we were in, and she came back to the hospital with us. She told me then that they were driving all civilians to the Velepromet compound and that my father and mother-in-law had already been taken there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like you to take a look at the next footage which is at 65 ter 4986.3, at tab 21. That is, tab J for the interpreters, and it will start at the 1 hour, 33 minutes, and 44 seconds mark. And I believe we can start, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Driver: ... most of the civilians have already been evacuated, you know. Today ... you saw it when they arrived -- "Doctor Bosanac: Wait, that's my mum. Just a moment, please. Where is Granny Milica" --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What do we see here, Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the moment as I was returning from Negoslavci when the car was stopped so that I could take my mother with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And the -- I mean, we will see more in a second, but in relation to the soldier who's accompanying there, on the left side of his shoulder what do you see on his shoulder?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really see it well, but it must be some kind of rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's keep playing the clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Doctor Bosanac: -- and the grandpa? "Mom: ... they came to the gas station in a red car. "Doctor Bosanac: Where, which gas station? "JNA Officer: This gas station, everybody's being evacuated, later ... "Doctor Bosanac: Please, can you take me back, those are my mother and father-in-law. "JNA Officer: Everybody is being evacuated. They are going to Velepromet, that's why we are evacuating them. "Doctor Bosanac: To Velepromet? "JNA Officer: Bogdan, can it --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I hear the -- someone says, "Bogdan" -- well, first of all, can you tell us what you see on this image?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the footage of a conversation between the JNA officer and myself and Bogdan Kuzmic, who is in military uniform with a helmet on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In which part of the screen can we see Bogdan Kuzmic? You can't really mark it, if you could just tell us.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left side in this still.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we still play it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Bogdan Kuzmic: Listen good, she is my neighbour, once was and always will be. "Doctor Bosanac: Don't get upset, Bogdan, everything will be all right ... "JNA Officer: Can you see to it, her father and mother-in-law have gone to the gas station? "Doctor Bosanac: ... you know where that is ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we just saw a soldier tapping you on your back. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that. Bogdan Kuzmic lived near to my apartment building, and before the war he worked at the reception in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We'll rewind this just a little bit to make sure who the person is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: A little bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So I just wanted to identify who was the person tapping you on your back there.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise that it may be Bogdan, although I cannot see clearly or recall things off the cuff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine. Thank you, Doctor. Now, this took place, as you described, right after you had met with Mile Mrksic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned to Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did the JNA officer who is at the right, were you aware of which unit he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask to tender this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 4986.3 will be Exhibit P1462.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, earlier you told us that before leaving the hospital for Negoslavci the first JNA soldiers had arrived. Upon your return, can you tell the Court who was in control at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, in control? I was still the manager of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. You were still the director of the hospital on that day; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, I would like you to look at the next clip which is 65 ter 4989.4 at tab 99. For the interpreters, it is tab F.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They could have gone home, if they were allowed to, but we are in the war and there is no chance that a slightly wounded person might go home; they have to stay and wait for evacuation. The biggest problem is that [indiscernible] was done today, but then again it was not done, and we hope that tomorrow it will finally be carried out because we have here the first [indiscernible] gangrene, infections, there is no water ... you will see it for yourselves. The things that are --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, who are you talking to, do you know?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was addressing those JNA officers who had come that afternoon to the hospital, but there was still no ICRC, only in the early afternoon did Major Sljivancanin come to the hospital. I believe he's not in this footage. I saw him first in the yard of the hospital, and he started the evacuation of civilians from the hospital. I protested and insisted that the wounded be the first to be evacuated once the ICRC arrives; however, he was very resolute. He was adamant and arrogant, and he said that from that moment on he was in charge of the hospital and he had to evacuate civilians first. That was on the Monday, the 19th, around 7.00, and only around 7.00 p.m. did the first representative of the ICRC arrive at the hospital, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did for the hear the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, let me clarify a few little bits the answer you just gave us. First of all, at the beginning of your answer you told us that Major Sljivancanin started the evacuation of the civilians from the hospital. Are you aware of where he was taking the civilians from the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time I didn't know. I learned later that they took everyone to Velepromet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And then towards the end of your answer, you said this was Monday the 19th, around 7.00.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not Monday. It was Tuesday. Tuesday, the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, around what time did Major Sljivancanin begin this evacuation of the civilians?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the afternoon, around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m. I don't know exactly, but it was still in daylight, soon after I returned from Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And around what time did the representative of the ICRC arrive?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 7.00 p.m., also accompanied by Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And the interpreters didn't catch the name of the ICRC representative. What was his name?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bossinger or Borsinger. I don't know exactly how to spell it. You'll find it probably in the earlier documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I move on, Your Honours, may I ask for this clip to be tendered, this was 65 ter 4989.4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the clip will be Exhibit P1463. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I show you now, Doctor, the next clip which is 4989.6 at tab 99. And that is tab G for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Djuro Srenk: There is no water --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Pause, please. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before we move on, Doctor, do you recognise this individual on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is our handyman from the technical staff of the hospital, Djuro Srenk was his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how long had he worked for the hospital at the time, in November 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of years. I can't say exactly, but a number of years. He was the handyman at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And between the months of September and November was he also working at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He worked throughout at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court whether Mr. Srenk is still alive?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was killed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you play the rest of the clip, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Djuro Srenk: -- we have no water. It is a disease cesspool, up to 500, 700 ... How long has it been, since they arrived? There are maybe a thousand patients and these are the people who all go to the toilet there."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this short clip which was 4989.6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 4989.6 will be Exhibit P1464. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we play the next clip which is 4989.10 at tab 99. And this is tab H for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: As a Frenchman, what are you doing in Vukovar?"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Pause here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this person, Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a patient, Jean-Michel Nicolier, who was a volunteer on the Vukovar defence, and he was at the hospital as one of the wounded waiting for evacuation like everyone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know with a happened to him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was also taken away on the 20th November, but I don't think he has been identified to date as one of those killed at Ovcara. I think he's still on record as a missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we keep playing the rest of the video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Jean-Michel Nicolier: I came as a volunteer and we lost. This is the first time I see them this close to me."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, do you recognise the soldier who just entered the image at this time, which is at 20 seconds of this clip?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Bogdan Kuzmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep playing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: Are you afraid? "Jean-Michel Nicolier: I'm not afraid. Soldiers are soldiers. I am a soldier as well. Of course, there are stupid people on all sides. What can you do? That's the way it is. I cannot, just because I'm French, pass 'in between the raindrops.' If I hadn't seen all this, I'd be gone a long time ago. But I'm here and I'll stay here, for better or worse ... in the good and the bad. There."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this clip which is 4989.10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, 4989.10 will be Exhibit P1465.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can I show you a last clip which is 4989.11 at tab 21, and for the interpreters that is tab I. The clip, I believe, will be in German but we have transcripts both in B/C/S and English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Ivan Herman: I don't know what was happening, who was with whom, how, and so on ... I don't know anything."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's also one of the wounded people. Herman was his name, wounded in the leg. He was at the hospital as well awaiting evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Was Herman his first or last name?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His last name. Ivan Herman is his full name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure any more whether he was identified as one of the victims from Ovcara - I'm not sure - or he's still recorded as missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can keep playing the video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: Do you know what the city is like now? "Ivan Herman: I know, I know. It's destroyed."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, may I tender this last clip which was 4989.11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P1466.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you explained that at 7.00 Mr. Borsinger from the ICRC arrived with Mr. Sljivancanin. Can you tell us what you -- well, what was your interaction with both these men at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the two of them, there was also one physician and an interpreter, a woman interpreter. I said the conditions in the hospital were very hard, that we had been awaiting the evacuation for a week, that we had prepared everything. They asked me if I had a list of people. I said yes, we had made a list of all the wounded, complete with diagnosis. They asked us to hand them those lists and we did. I thought, in fact, that the ICRC would need only one list and we could keep the rest; however, Major Sljivancanin insisted to get all the copies of the lists. He asked if we also had a list of the staff. I said no. It hadn't seemed to us necessary. So we made a list of the staff that evening. Mr. Borsinger said, after touring the hospital and after they saw what the situation was like, he said they had to leave and they would come back the next morning, which surprised me quite a lot because I expected them as the ICRC, once they arrived, to stay and take care of the hospital. However, he said he had to leave and he would be back at 8.00 the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Did he expect -- did he explain to you why he had to leave?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me anything. He just said he had to leave. I had expected them to stay, but he said they would be back in the morning and had to return to Belgrade. That worried me very seriously after everything we had gone through, but considering that he had seen the situation with his own eyes and we had turned over all the lists of the wounded, I certainly wasn't expecting that the evacuation would not be handled by them and that everything that later happened would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, did he -- what choice did he have to stay at the hospital that evening?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course he could have stayed at the hospital, and we expected him to. I don't know what he discussed with Sljivancanin and what Sljivancanin had told him, but if I had been in his shoes, I would have stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when you were touring the hospital with him, you said he saw the situation. Who else was with you and Mr. Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Sljivancanin and that Swiss doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. How long did he stay at the hospital that evening?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About an hour, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And was there any discussion in relation to the evacuation agreement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, but as I said, he still left. It's obvious that everybody interpreted that agreement in their own way. I don't know what organising evacuation meant to him. It would be a good idea for this Court to call him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, can I ask you to look at the next video-clip which is 65 ter 4989.5 at tab 21. And for the interpreters it is tab K. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Nicolas Borsinger: We are --"

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Do you know who this person is?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Borsinger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Let's keep playing.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Nicolas Borsinger: We are present here to remind the warring parties of the humanitarian measures that need to be undertaken for this kind of operation to proceed properly."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, with -- with the end of the conflict you talked to us about the fact that there was an evacuation agreement and that the possibility of an evacuation was always there.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier that there was word of an evacuation in the days leading to the fall of Vukovar. How do you interpret the words that we have heard now where Mr. Borsinger is saying that the ICRC's present here to remind the warring parties of the humanitarian measures to be undertaken in this kind of operation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot comment. I don't know what he meant by that. It's obvious that he as the ICRC representative did not implement the evacuation agreement that was endorsed in Zagreb by the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when he left that evening, what did he tell you about the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he would be back the next morning at 8.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And did he tell you for what purpose he would return the next day at 8.00?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To carry out the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you heard that he said that he would return to carry out the evacuation, what did that mean to you at that moment?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hoped that things would happen like he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this clip which is 4989.5, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 4989.5 will be Exhibit P1467.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, after he left that evening, was anything in particular taking place at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, Sljivancanin came looking for a lady doctor to see if she was at the hospital. Then he took her away for an interview. Then an officer came for me. A JNA officer came to take me somewhere for an interview, and he took me again to Negoslavci. There I was interrogated by Sljivancanin and another -- I don't know what he was exactly. A man wearing a black uniform. Perhaps he was an investigator or a policeman, I don't know. At any rate, they were questioning me there; it lasted for about an hour. They questioned me about the whereabouts of the Vukovar defence commanders, their identity. I expected to be taken back to the hospital; however, they did not take me back. They left me to spend the night at Negoslavci, at the schoolhouse which they used as a military hospital and a barracks. I saw a lot of troops there. I stayed there until 6.00 a.m., when they picked me up again and took me away in a military vehicle where Marin Vidic was there, and they took me back to the hospital on Wednesday, on the 20th, around 6.00 that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I return to this questioning that you referred to by Sljivancanin. You said that he asked you about the whereabouts of the Vukovar defence commanders. In what way did he behave towards you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was arrogant. I said I had no idea where the defence commanders were or who they were. He was very angry, very arrogant. He wanted to know who had killed his young soldiers, and I asked in my turn why he had brought them to Vukovar in the first place. He was very angry. I asked to be taken back to the hospital, but they refused. They said it was dangerous to drive by night, and they left me in Negoslavci until the morning. I later heard that that night many people were taken away for interrogation. Some of them never returned, like Branko Lukenda and Tomislav Hegedus, men who worked for the police. They were taken away that night, and they never returned. Nobody knows where they ended up. Also, our medical technician Marko Mandic was taken away that night. Nobody knows where he ended up or where his grave is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us that you heard that many people were taken away. Were you informed of who took them away?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as Marko Mandic is concerned, I heard Bogdan Kuzmic was the one who took him away. I heard that from Marko's wife. I don't know about the others. They were probably taken away by some members of the army as I was taken by them to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, earlier we saw footage with Bogdan Kuzmic at the hospital. You also told us that Veselin Sljivancanin was at the hospital. Could you give an idea to the Court as to how many JNA soldiers or officers were present at the hospital on the afternoon of the 19th?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And where did you see these soldiers or officers?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers were posted at the entrance to the hospital, at different entrances to the hospital, and they walked around the hallways, the yard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you're saying they were posted at the entrances of the hospital. For what purpose?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, even before I went to Negoslavci the first time when that first officer came to the hospital, I asked if they were able to guarantee safety to the hospital pending the arrival of the ICRC. And back then he posted those soldiers - they were military police officers - at the entrances to the hospital, and they were there throughout the time that I was there until they took me away to detention on the Wednesday, the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Your Honours, I notice the time. It might be an appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, we'll take the first break and come back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of the court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, let me update you in relation to the motion that we're filing this morning. We are in a position to file within the next hour or so. If I do finish my examination-in-chief before the end of the day, I suspect that we can begin cross-examination with the possibility of me doing further re-examination-in-chief tomorrow morning once the Defence has had the time to read and digest our motion, respond to that. Would that be an acceptable procedure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that would be the only possible procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you expect to finish your examination-in-chief before the end of the hearing today?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm hoping to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You're hoping to,

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, I'd like us to go now to the morning of the 20th of November. You told us that that morning you were taken back by car with Marin Vidic. Can you tell us again at what time exactly you returned to the hospital on the morning of the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely 6.00 when the driver came to pick me up with a JNA vehicle. He took me back to the hospital. I was back there at around 6.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, on that morning what was the situation in relation to shelling and artillery fire which you described throughout the months of October and November? What was the situation on the morning of the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 20th in the morning there was no more shooting any more. I couldn't hear any detonations or shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And I failed to ask you this earlier, but what was the situation on the 19th of November in relation to shelling and shooting?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear any explosions or shells on the 19th either. It was a quiet time as regards explosions and shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And in your assessment, what was -- what were the conditions in relation to an evacuation on the 19th? Were there conditions actually?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were conditions in place, preconditions in place. If the ICRC and ECMM had come on the 18th, as had been agreed upon, on the 19th evacuation may well have been possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, returning to this issue of the 20th, you said that it was at 6.30 to be precise that you were back at the hospital. What happened at the hospital at that moment?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in my office waiting for the ICRC. The phone rang several times. There was a JNA officer with me in the office who would not let me answer it. He answered every call, responding that he was an officer of the victorious army and that I could not answer the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, did anything specific happen shortly after this -- what you just described?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: An officer arrived asking which large room could be used to hold a meeting with the staff. The only larger room was the casting room where there were no patients. I was taken there, by which time all of the staff had been brought there as well, or most of them, most of the people working at the hospital in Vukovar. It was there that Major Sljivancanin gave a speech in the presence of another five military persons who were introduced to us as military doctors. The JNA had its own VMA, which is the Military Medical Academy. The physicians in question were in JNA uniform. Sljivancanin said that as of that day, the hospital would be under the competence of the VMA and that all of the staff who were gathered there could decide whether they wanted to remain working in the hospital or if they wished to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, around about what time did this meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 7.30. As far as I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Half an hour. I was returned to my office at around 8.00. I sat there for a while. A JNA representative arrived and said that Marin Vidic and I were to go with him. Marin Vidic was with me in the same room. The two of us went outside, walked down the line of the medical personnel who were lined up outside awaiting evacuation. I was convinced at the time that we were going to be taken to a range and evacuation, but we were actually taken to a detention unit in the barracks, the JNA barracks in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, that morning, which -- which international organisation, if any, were present at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anyone then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us that Sljivancanin said that as of that day the hospital would be under the competence of the military hospital. During this meeting, were you aware of what was happening outside the room?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you told us a moment ago that when you left, you saw the staff lined up waiting for the evacuation. Was there anything else that you noticed at that moment?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We went past the line of medical personnel to the military vehicle which took us away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you say that you were then taken with Marin Vidic to the JNA barracks. How much time did it take from the hospital to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ten to 15 minutes, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And where were you taken once you arrived at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To a room on the first floor. A military policeman was inside and stayed there throughout while we were seated there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how long were you held in that room?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Who, if anyone, visited you in that room?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A JNA representative came and brought in some food, some cold cuts, but other than that no one came to talk to us until that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And were you able to speak to the international monitors or the ICRC on that day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to show you a clip now which is 65 ter 4989.9 at tab 21. For the interpreters, that is tab N.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "So you [indiscernible] you can worry also about his soldiers who are [indiscernible] killing today. It's not your attitude" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't find it under N.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with this footage?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it later upon my arrival in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And are you -- can you tell us where this is taking place, where this footage was filmed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was taken somewhere in the centre of town, to the -- to the right is Mr. Borsinger, and to the left is Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we keep playing the video -- before we do that, did we locate the translation for the interpreters? Okay. It is indeed under tab N. Do the interpreters have the transcript which starts at 10 minutes, 57 seconds?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I believe that the first two seconds might have been missing but it is correct. Let's keep playing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: "You're not welcome. "Veselin Sljivancanin: [Interpretation] Sir, my soldiers lost their life here tonight. Sir, there's a war here. "Nicolas Borsinger: All we knew was that there was a convoy leaving the hospital and at the same time they are trying to deny us access to the hospital and that ... so, in such circumstances we couldn't but ask what is really going on "Veselin Sljivancanin: [Interpretation] [indiscernible] behave the way before me [indiscernible] security and peace and you're causing problems for me. If you don't like it, go ahead and go back. Go where you like it. I'm ashamed that you're treating me this way. I gave you everything you asked for."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, the previous evening you told us that you saw Borsinger and Sljivancanin at the hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How would you compare -- well, first of all, how was he speaking or addressing -- or how was Sljivancanin addressing Borsinger that evening when you saw them?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean how? In a rather normal tone. He didn't shout like in the last clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And did you recognise anybody else on that video-clip besides Sljivancanin and Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this clip which is 4989.9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 4989.9 will be Exhibit P1468.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, earlier we saw the evacuation agreement, and you read out the part which dealt with the principle of neutrality. How was this applied on the 20th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you explain to us how it wasn't?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't, because neither the ICRC nor the ECMM were present on the morning the 20th when Major Sljivancanin said that as of that moment on the hospital was under the competence of the JNA and the VMA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like you to take a look at the next clip which is 65 ter 4799.11. This is at tab 91. For the interpreters it should be tab O.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Nicolas Borsinger: This went on for quite a long time. I would just like to say that last night -- in fact yesterday afternoon, we made agreement with the JNA which was represented by General Raseta and the Croatian government. The object of this agreement was to neutralise the Vukovar Hospital in accordance with Article 15 of the Geneva Convention. I will go into detail about this agreement. The objective was for it to come into force at 20:00 hours last night on the 19th of November. According to this agreement, access to the hospital and surrounding buildings was limited to patients and military personnel as the first category; the second category were civilians who did not participate in the war; the third category was the medical staff; and the fourth was the delegates of the International Red Cross. Point three prohibited bringing any military equipment into the hospital. Gentlemen, you know and you can see what actually happened here. Except for these four categories of the people we -- of people we mentioned, no one else was allowed to enter the hospital unless they had a permit issued by the International Red Cross. You saw how this agreement was sought. Secondly, we said that the hospital needed to be clearly marked with a red cross. The last item is exceptionally important because it says that the Croatian authorities and the JNA will provide full co-operation with the International Red Cross in order to implement the agreement. You probably noticed that the International Committee was -- or, rather, was not able to carry out the task it was entrusted with, and therefore it cannot be held responsible for this morning's events. And now I do not know, because I was prevented from entering the hospital area."

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We can pause here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, that morning could you -- did you know who exactly took you from the hospital to the JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A JNA officer. I don't know what his name is or what his rank was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And are you aware of who was -- who was in charge at that moment of the JNA officers at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Sljivancanin was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask for 4799.11 to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 4799.11 will be Exhibit P1469.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, on that day were there any members of your family at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My mother was there, as well as my in-laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court what happened to them on that day?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My mother said that a soldier came in the hospital and said that all of those who could walk should go out. My father-in-law came out of the basement where they had been awaiting evacuation. He was elderly and sick and had problems with his legs. He went outside to stretch his legs and was taken away. For a long time he was considered missing, until he was identified in 1996 as having been killed at Ovcara. My mother and my mother-in-law came out with the rest of civilians and went to Zagreb. When I came after a prisoner exchange, I found them in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Doctor, you told us that your father-in-law was killed at Ovcara. For the record, could you tell us his name?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father-in-law's name was Dragutin Bosanac. When he was being identified, we saw a forensic medical report in the English language. His identification was carried out by American pathologists. In the identification report, one could clearly see that he was the person in question given his previous ailments and the artefacts found next to his skeleton, as well as clothes, home keys, some documents he had with him. The cause of death was through wounds to the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, we know what happened to name of patients and persons, other men from the hospital on the day of the 20th of November. I would like to ask you of those who were later found to be killed at Ovcara, were there any staff members of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At Ovcara during exhumations, 200 bodies were dug out. Out of those, 193 have been identified. Among them there were the wounded and defenders and civilians and hospital staff, including Djuro Srenk whom you saw in the footage. On top of that there were some youngsters, minors, a nurse's son, a cleaning lady's son and husband who worked at the hospital during the war. Basically everyone who was taken from the hospital. It isn't all of them, though, because even to date 58 persons are still being sought out of those taken from the hospital.
