It includes 33 wounded persons and civilians, policemen such as Branko Lukenda and Tomislav Hegedus, and then the medical technician Marko Mandic. Two hundred and ninety-six people are still missing from the town of Vukovar; out of that number, 58 of them were taken from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, at this time I would like to show you a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I do that, Your Honours, what I'm about to show is the list of identified victims from the Ovcara mass grave. Prior to the witness coming to the court, I did ask her to identify which of those were hospital staff members and family members of the hospital staff. So this is a list that is pre-marked. I've shared this information with the Defence so that we save time in the courtroom rather than having the witness mark them one by one. I just want to ensure that before I proceed that this is accepted by the Defence and by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We've agreed to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. May I display the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 5846.1. The original 5846 was at - let me tell you the tab - tab 107. Very well. Can we enlarge this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, are you familiar with the list you see in front of you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. First of all, could you tell us what this -- what the markings we see in handwritten form are?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They represent how these people were related to the medical staff in the hospital. The first person is the husband of a lady who worked in the hospital. Then the one marked with HS, Ilija Asadjanin, he was a driver working for the hospital; Ivan Bainrauh was a mechanical engineer who was the head of technical personnel at the hospital. Josip Balog was the son of our laundry woman; he was 16 at the time. Dragutin Balog was the laundry woman's husband and Josip's father. He was a sick man. He had cancer of his throat and he had a prosthesis, and on my permission they were accommodated at the hospital together with the laundry lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, for the understanding of the Trial Chamber, could you tell us what FHS and what HS stand for?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: FHS stands for family hospital staff. HS stands for hospital staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. So FHS, family hospital staff, means that these were members of the family of the hospital staff member, is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please. Do we see three more markings on this page?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Tomislav Baumgertner was the son of one of our nurses. He was born in 1973, which means that he was 17. Then Dragutin Bosanac, my father-in-law. Tomislav Bosanac is a relative, a nephew of my husband who was accompanying his wounded wife. She was a nurse and she was seriously wounded at the hospital at that time. I personally cautioned Major Sljivancanin that the seriously wounded always have somebody to accompany them, and this Tomislav was accompanying his seriously injured wife, but he was taken away anyway and executed at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's look at one more page. Can we go to the next one, please? Here we see two more markings at page 3.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan Buovac was a driver. Petar Furundzija was the husband of one of our employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And is it correct to say that on the remaining pages we also have these two terms, HS and FHS, used throughout the document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed this before this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could we go to the last page, page 12. On this page we see two more markings, and we see on one of the patients that the name Dominik Zeravica has been circled. Can you tell us if there's anything particular about this victim?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning this victim, there is a nota bene of the commission for the missing. He was identified by DNA analysis; however, the family did not accept this finding. So the commission still has him on record as a missing person.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I make an application to tender this marked version which is 5846.1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 5846.1 will be Exhibit P1470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, are you able to tell us how many of the killed persons at Ovcara were hospital patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We still don't know about many of them. Not all have been identified out of the 193. Ninety-two were wounded according to what we know today. Considering all the medical records from the Vukovar Hospital have still not been returned and our -- and are somewhere in the archive of the military court in Belgrade, all that we know for sure is that the list of the wounded made on the 20th November that we were able to send to the Ministry of Health, and according to the lists in the notebooks that were returned to us two years ago with the mediation of the President of Serbia, that was when a smaller part of our documentation was returned, including notebooks of the head nurse giving exact information about all the wounded, complete with the date of admission and the reason why they were admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, out of the identified 193 victims, do you know out of that number how many were hospital patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ninety-three, I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Could we display the 65 ter 636, which is at tab 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a list of the wounded from the Vukovar Hospital who have been identified at Ovcara. From all the identified -- from all the available information I prepared this list for one of the trials here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: We see the continuation of this list going down up to -- well, in the B/C/S version to 75, I believe. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can we go to the third page, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And the very last name here is at number 97, I believe. Is that number accurate, Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the number is accurate, except that we did not have documentation for all these persons showing that they were wounded, but we do know that they were taken from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. If we go to page 4, which is the next page in both versions, can you tell us what we are looking at here?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a questionnaire that we filled during the war concerning all wounded persons, and we sent it to the main medical staff at the Ministry of Health so that by 6 November we were able to e-mail this data. After that date the communications broke down and we were unable to send any more lists of the wounded that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, we see here the name of the person, gender, date of birth, et cetera, and then we see if they have a hospitalisation diagnosis. Could you explain to us what is the diagnosis, please?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Vul explos genus sinos," that means a blast wound to the left knee and lower leg. The data was entered on the 21st of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how were you able to prepare this certificate? Specifically, how were you able to collect this information in relation to the wound?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This data was entered in fact based on the medical documentation that we had for every patient. The description of the condition, doctor's findings, et cetera. The problem was with those who were brought in after the 6th of November. We were no longer able to enter that kind of information and their medical records were taken away and still had not been returned. All of the information we have about them comes from those notebooks, the notebooks from the head nurse that we got back only two years ago, and from those notebooks we were able to fill in some more information, and the medical records have still not been returned to the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, at the beginning of this document, the first thing we saw was a list of the wounded with 97 patients, and now we see a casualty certificate. Is there a casualty certificate in this bundle for every patient listed from 1 to 97?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From one of the previous trials here in The Hague I prepared protocols, and in the cases where we had death certificate, I was able to include it as well as the photograph with the personal details for every person that I was able to get from the association of mothers searching for their missing sons and fathers from lists of camp inmates. So I prepared these search protocols for those persons who were at the time detained, dead, or missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, in relation to my specific question, I was asking you whether there is a similar casualty certificate for every one of the 97 listed people at the beginning of the document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I ask to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 636 will be Exhibit P1471.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you explained to us earlier that on the 20th of November you were kept at the JNA barracks the entire day. What happened to you next?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On Wednesday, the 20th November?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening of the 20th at the barracks I was interrogated for the first time. There were video cameras there. I was questioned about what went on at the Vukovar Hospital during the war. After that, together with Dr. Njavro and Anto Maric [as interpreted] I was taken in a police vehicle to the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. In the morning of the 21st, very early, I was brought to that prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How long were you kept in the prison in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About three weeks, perhaps a little less.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And on the 20th of November -- oh, sorry, on the 21st of November, were you informed as to why you were taken to Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And upon your arrival at Sremska Mitrovica, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the prison there was an officer of the Yugoslav Army who said I had been brought there to be investigated about the situation in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And once you arrive at the -- at the prison, where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was taken to a room -- in fact, Dr. Njavro, this Ante Maric [as interpreted] and I were taken there together. Dr. Njavro was forced to stand against the wall looking down and with his hands behind his back, whereas Anto Aric [as interpreted] was severely beaten by the prison guards. That shook me up terribly, and I protested with the commander of that prison over the beating. I underwent the procedure of questioning. That first night I spent in the solitary cell, and as of the next day, the afternoon of the next day, the 21st of November, and the two and a half weeks that followed I was in a room with 86 women from Vukovar. Like all the prisoners, I had a very hard time there. I had to write a statement describing all that happened in Vukovar. I wrote a 116-page statement. That statement is also available to this Court, and it was only at one of the previous trials that I was able to see it again, here in The Hague. The last two days I was taken from Mitrovica to the military investigation prison in Belgrade where a procedure was instituted against me. However, they did not prove any charges. I had an assigned duty counsel, and the only thing they charged me with was that I sent out appeals and reports the world over --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- describing how the Yugoslav People's Army was an aggressor, criminal army. That was the charge against me. However, I was released as part of a prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can I take you back to the beginning of that answer where you told us that you were -- well, that Anto Aric was severely beaten by prison guards. Are you able to tell the Judges to which institution the prison guards belonged to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Aric, not Maric but Aric, beginning with an A.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And are you able to tell the Judges to which institution the prison guards belonged to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. I don't know. They were prison guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And you spoke to the commander. Did you know to which institution he belonged?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us briefly about the conditions, that you were held in a cell the first night and that you were held with 86 women from Vukovar. Can you describe this second room, I suppose? Where were you held exactly with 86 women from Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a large room, like a large classroom or a small gym where we slept on the floor, on mattresses. And there was also a smaller room next door with toilet and washing facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And are you able to tell the Judges how large was this room?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixty-six -- well, I don't know exactly how large it was. It was perhaps 20 by 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court how much food you were provided during your detention?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received food in large cauldrons and pots, stews with peppers and stuff, very tasteless, stinking food, sometimes bread and tea.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court about the hygienic conditions during your detention?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bad. I told you there was only this one bathroom with cold water. It was impossible, horrible conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You also told us that you gave a lengthy statement. Can you tell us who you gave this statement to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every day I was interrogated by an officer of the Yugoslav Army who introduced himself as Captain Branko. I don't know if that was his real name. At any rate, he questioned me every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just in relation to his rank, did you say Captain Branko?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And how was this statement prepared?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it in longhand. He put questions to me, and I answered those questions. I had to sign every page, and he put a number and each page. I wanted to write in that statement everything that I had written earlier in my appeals, but he told me not to write it when I wanted to but at the end of the statement. He said I should just focus on answering the questions. I cannot remember exactly, but in fact I believe -- I believe that statement is in existence somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And could you tell us generally how you were treated by Captain Branko?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, compared to the others, he treated me rather well. They did not mistreat me mentally or physically. I was able to say everything I wanted to. I was able to smoke as much as I wanted to, which was important to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us that you were held in a room with other women. Were there men held at the prison in Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of the prisoners were men. When I was brought there I didn't actually know that, but I heard in one of the following days from the women with whom I shared that room how they had ended up there. They were from Sajmiste and from Mitnica, and they told me how their sons and husbands had been brought there. I cleaned the corridor with another woman, and I saw a lot of bandages and bits of plaster casts, and I thought that there must be some wounded people there. However, I later found out that nobody from the hospital had been brought there. Instead, the wounded from other shelters, from Borovo Komerc had been brought there. There were among the women the sick and infirm. There were women with smaller children. There was one woman with very little children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the men, were you aware of the conditions under which they were kept?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that. I was able to see that for myself, and I heard things from others and read reports. My husband was there. They were severely beaten and mistreated. I could hear by night the screams, the cries, and I kept protesting with this Colonel Branko over the treatment of prisoners. They were physically mistreated. They were starved. There is plenty of testimony about that that you can get if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, just before we take the break, now you said Colonel Branko and originally we heard Captain Branko. Which of the two is it?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't know what his rank was. I think he was a captain, but I don't know really. Perhaps you can find out from other witness statements, because he interrogated a lot of people. I can't remember. I think he was a captain, and the Colonel was the one who took us into the prison, the one who was the prison commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And one final question before the break. Do you know approximately how -- the age of this Captain or Colonel Branko?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say precisely. Around 50, perhaps, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, is this the time for the break? No. We have another 15 minutes. Sorry. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Dr. Bosanac, for having given you false hope, but we have another 15 minutes before the break. Now, during your detention, were you visited by anyone?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited -- I was visited by European observers, European Monitors, perhaps a week into my stay at that prison. Those monitors who were supposed to come to the Vukovar Hospital that day instead came to see me at the prison. A meeting was organised, attended by representatives of the prison, myself, and they the monitors. I can't remember anything particular about that meeting except that I saw five or six of them in those white and blue uniforms of the ECMM. And I was visited also by representatives of the ICRC. In fact, they visited everyone. They took down messages addressed to families and brought some lists where families indicated details necessary for the search. There was also a visit from physicians from Belgrade who came from the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade, high-ranking officials.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, in relation to the beginning of your answer, you mentioned European observers or monitors. Are you aware of what was the purpose of their visit?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they wanted to see for themselves who exactly was kept in that prison, where I was in view of our previous correspondence. On the second day of my stay in that prison, it was a Friday, the 22nd, I heard on the radio -- the women in the prison had a radio, so I heard that the Vatican was searching for us. I heard it on a show at 7.00, Radio Vatican broadcasting in Croatian. They were searching for Dr. Sinisa Glavasevic [as interpreted] from the Vukovar Hospital. They were looking for priests and nuns. That was the first sign that somebody does know where we are after all and that they were looking for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, the record reflects that you said that: "They were searching for Dr. Sinisa Glavasevic from the Vukovar Hospital"; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Physicians from the Vukovar Hospital and Sinisa Glavasevic, who was a journalist.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. Now, could you tell us a little bit about the circumstances of your release from Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a bit over two weeks of interrogation, on a Sunday the prison warden or prison commander came and said that I should pack up and that I was to be sent onwards. I was assigned to a bus where some other prisoners were, including my husband. We were taken to the ministry -- military investigating prison in Belgrade where I spent another two days, after which I was exchanged alongside others as part of a prisoner exchange. We were exchanged for certain members of the counter-intelligence service from Zagreb who will -- who were called the Labrador Group as far as I remember. We were put on a plane and flew from Belgrade to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, during the period of your detention, what charges, if any, were brought against you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Mitrovica, I wasn't charged with anything. I simply had to draft a statement and answer questions about the wounded, the burials. When I was in Belgrade for the two days, I was being accused for -- of sending appeals and setting up health care during the aggression against Vukovar as well as for having drafted appeals that I sent out to the world saying that the JNA was an aggressor army. It has been my argument consistently and still is, saying it was a criminal army. A military court of sorts was put up there, and I became a bit scared at the time, thinking that it would prolong my stay in detention. Defence counsel was appointed ex officio, and he approached me in a very calm way. He was a military person, and he said that I shouldn't be worried, that I will not spend a long time in jail because I was only charged --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with a verbal offence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, I'd like you to take a look at the next document which is 65 ter 5128, at tab 106. Doctor, do you see the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, this document is dated the 11th of December, 1991, and at the top here it indicates that Dr. Vesna Bosanac, yourself, and Dr. Juraj Njavro were released on the 10th of December in a prisoner exchange. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, but I still can't find the part you read out. Yes. Now, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in the B/C/S version can we go to page 2. We can remain on page 1 in the English version. At the top of the page in the B/C/S version you can see here that there is a paragraph which says that there is still no further news of the journalist Sinisa Glavasevic.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Earlier you mentioned to us that when the EC monitors visited you they were looking for hospital doctors and Sinisa Glavasevic. Do you know why Mr. Glavasevic was -- why people were looking for him?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I suppose that similar kind of appeals were sent for him as was done with regard to myself, Dr. Njavro, and other hospital doctors. I believe appeals were sent by our colleagues and friends. By the same token, journalists were probably looking for Sinisa Glavasevic. He reported daily over the radio and fax messages, sending reports to his association of journalists. I suppose that is way they asked that he be released as well as Branimir Polovina, who was with Sinisa Glavasevic. They worked for the Croatian Rade Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In fact, if we turn to page 1 in the B/C/S version. Yes, here in the middle of the page you can see a list of five names starting with yours, Dr. Njavro, followed by Sinisa Glavasevic, Branimir Polovina who you just mentioned, as well as Marin Vidic-Bili. Do you know what happened to him because I believe you told us he was also taken to Sremska Mitrovica with you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Marin Vidic-Bili [Realtime transcript read in error "Vidovic"] was taken to Mitrovica. He was imprisoned there the whole period until he was exchanged on the 13th [Realtime transcript read in error "3rd"] of August, 1992, when most were exchanged. It was a large exchange following a series of negotiations. Many Vukovar citizens had been exchanged earlier, say in December and then in May 1992. I took part in all of those exchanges because we were constantly looking for those who were missing, and I was also looking for members of my father-in-law's family. I looked for many people and travelled around the globe to Brussels, London, Washington in the US, as well as in Zagreb. When I was there, I worked as an advisor for humanitarian issues in the Ministry of Health. I took part in many a negotiation. Marin Vidic was exchanged as part of the large exchange on the 13th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just one clarification, Doctor. At the beginning of the answer you told us you were exchanged on the 3rd of August. Now you're saying the 13th. Are you aware of the exact date?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And just a clarification --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or the 14th. There was one single exchange in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: At the beginning of your answer, I see the name has been recorded as Marin Vidovic, but you did clarify it's Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marin Vidic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 5128 will be Exhibit P1472.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May this be an appropriate time for the break, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It is. Dr. Bosanac, this is our second break. We will come back at 12.45. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Demirdjian, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I'd like to ask you a question in relation to a matter I asked you earlier today, so I will take you back to before your detention in Sremska Mitrovica. If you remember earlier, I asked you what was the situation on the 19th and the 20th in relation to the shelling. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are you able to assist the Court in telling us what was the situation on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning on the 18th, things were quiet. It was a nice sunny day, much like today. We were all awaiting evacuation. However, no one reported, no one came, and then shelling started. They were -- the shells were coming from the left bank of the Danube. The explosive devices flew over the hospital and town. I don't know where they landed. It wasn't like any other day. There was less shooting, but still there was shelling on the 18th. On the 19th and the 20th, it was completely quiet. There was no more shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you said that the shelling was coming from the left bank of the Danube on the 18th of November, and they flew over the hospital. Do you know in which direction they were -- they were firing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Bogdanovci.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the second name. We didn't catch it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in the south-west part of town. I don't know exactly where the shells landed. I only know they did not land on the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: After Bogdanovci you mentioned another village which wasn't captured by the interpreters. Can you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Marinci is the closest village to Bogdanovci, towards Nustar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And do you know why the shelling began again on the 18th of November?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. Later on it was my impression that the shelling was done so that evacuation would not occur that day, as an excuse, because the ECMM observers who called me on the phone told me that they couldn't pass through as the JNA could not guarantee their safety since there was still combat. I really don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. I'd like to take you to the period after or following your release from the prison in Sremska Mitrovica. Could you tell the Court once you were flown from Belgrade to Croatia what did you do. Did you take up any functions?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I began working in the Ministry of Health as an advisor for humanitarian issues. I remained director of the medical centre of Vukovar in exile.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And as part of your role as an advisor on humanitarian issues, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My most important job was to look for those who were detained and missing and the wounded from the Vukovar Hospital. Then I was trying to assist all displaced persons, and I assisted in the setting up of the work of medical staff in exile as well as other tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: As part of your work to look for those who were detained and missing and wounded from the Vukovar Hospital, how were you able to work on this part of your function?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I worked a lot in the process of taking statements and testimony of those who had been detained and who had gone through the evacuation process from Vukovar. I also continued drafting appeals on the topic of what was happening with the wounded and their fate. I was often on the road visiting Lord Carrington, Cyrus Vance, Amnesty International in London. I went to Brussels and Paris to see Kouchner. I participated in the negotiations conducted by the ICRC with the Serbian Red Cross or of the then former Yugoslavia. It had to do with identifying those who were detained in Serbia. I attended all exchanges. I talked to many people, many detainees who were released. I wrote about it. I drafted reports. I held meetings with different organisations which were looking for the missing and detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you mentioned a moment ago that you participated in negotiations conducted by the ICRC. In which -- in what kind of a forum was this -- were these negotiations being held?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negotiating commissions were set up in Geneva and in Budapest and in Hungary. I read their reports, and for a while in the summer of 1992 I was also a member of one such commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Are you aware of when these negotiations were initiated?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These negotiations were initiated as early as December 1991. Based on the work of those commissions and negotiations, detainees were being released from many prisons already in 1991 and then in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. May I show you one of the minutes of such meetings. It is 65 ter 6402, at tab 115. Doctor, do you see these minutes on your screen?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: They indicate that these were held on the 2nd of April, 1992, in Pec. Can you tell us where Pec is located?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pec is a town in Hungary close to the Croatian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, first of all we see representatives of various parties. The first participants we see here are under the header Federal Executive Council. Can you tell us of which state or country that is?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose they were from the former Yugoslavia, as far as I can see from the names, although I don't know them personally. I know the members of the Croatian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And could you tell us very briefly who are the members of the Croatian delegation?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Ivan Simonovic, he was a member of the commission on behalf of Croatia. He is a lawyer by profession. Nenad Javornik was the secretary of the Croatian Red Cross. Ms. Dubravka Horvat was also from the Croatian Red Cross. Ivica Kopjar was the secretary of the Croatian Red Cross in Osijek. Dr. Davor Strinovic is a pathologist from the school of medicine of Zagreb university. He is an identification expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, towards the bottom of the page we see representatives of the Yugoslav People's Army. Are you familiar with the names here?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The names are familiar, although I don't know any of them personally. I only met those people at meetings that I attended on two occasions as part of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And at the bottom of the page we see the representatives of the ICRC. I think in the B/C/S version you only see one name the other two names are on the next page. Are these names that you are familiar with?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know personally this Paul Bonard who regularly took part in these meetings, and he was later involved in that large exchange of prisoners in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to take you to page 5 in both the English and the B/C/S version. In the B/C/S version we need to scroll down to the bottom part of the page. All the way down, please. Thank you very much. Doctor, do you see item number VI, "Information on the wounded of Vukovar Hospital"?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, here it is recorded that Dr. Simonovic commented that Croatia's side was unsatisfied with data received on wounded in Vukovar Hospital, and he indicates here that according to incomplete lists, it is considered that there were 390 wounded at the Vukovar Hospital. What can you tell us about this number and about what Dr. Simonovic is saying here?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you when we discussed this -- Dr. Hebrang and I when we talked on the phone discussing how many ambulances and vehicles needed to be prepared for the evacuation of the hospital, I told you that there were around 450 patients and wounded in the Vukovar Hospital, including 360 wounded and 46 very seriously injured who were immobile and lying in the intensive care unit, and the total of people in Vukovar Hospital was 700 or so. It's probably based on that information that Dr. Simonovic was seeking lists of all those patients and wounded awaiting evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next page in the B/C/S version. We can stay on the same page in the English version. In the top part of the page you see that there is a -- in the B/C/S version you can go to the top. Yeah. There is a record here saying that: "According to Dr. Simonovic, complete lists were handed over by Dr. Bosanac to Major Sljivancanin, in the presence of witnesses as well as a notebook and a computer with complete information." Can you give the Trial Chamber your comments in relation to this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this record is not quite accurate, because I did not hand over the computer or the medical records. I handed over to Mr. Borsinger in the presence of Mr. Sljivancanin all the lists of patients and wounded, whereas the computer and the medical records were all in my office awaiting evacuation. In the meantime when I was taken away, I came back. I learned that all this documentation was taken to Belgrade, because I saw in a Serbian weekly called Ilustrovana Politika an interview with a Dr. Stankovic from Belgrade, a pathologist who conducted identifications in Vukovar, and in that newspaper story and the photographs in it I saw that they had in their possession our computer which had remained at the hospital after they took me away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now -- yes. I'd like to take you to the bottom of that page in the B/C/S version, and in the English version we need to go to the next page, please. Do you see at the bottom of the page that there's a section where Colonel Starcevic -- well, his words are reported? Do you see that portion there at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see what's written at the bottom, that the Vukovar Hospital be given neutrality; however, this agreement was not accepted by the JNA because the ICRC required exclusive access to the hospital. The JNA came into the hospital and found 100 armed men who did not have a single -- and I can't see what else is written because it's the end of the page, but what is written here that there were 100 armed men in the hospital is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Just -- yes. You can see the rest of that paragraph there on the top of at that page. And it continues in saying that --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And there was no reason for them to be in the hospital, the example being Karlo Crk, director of the Vupik factory from Vukovar whose name was on the list of medical staff. First of all, it's not true that there were 100 armed people. Second, this Karlo Crk was in the hospital as a civilian. He had been working in the police preparing food, because before the war he worked at the slaughterhouse in Vupik as head of the slaughter-house, and he was preparing food and meat both for the police and the army, the Croatian Army, and the hospital. He was a civilian. He was not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, two paragraphs below that there's a sentence which reads as follows: "Colonel Starcevic asserted that Major Sljivancanin never got the said lists." What can you tell us about that? You told us earlier that you handed over the lists to Mr. Borsinger?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hand it over to Mr. Borsinger in the presence of Sljivancanin, the lists of patients and wounded, whereas the list of the medical staff was prepared by the administrator of that council, and the next morning I was taken away. So I don't know whether they had the list of staff or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. At the -- can we go to the next page in the B/C/S version. We can stay on the same page in the English version. And we can scroll down towards the bottom of that page. I'm sorry, this is not what I'm looking for in the B/C/S version. I'm looking for page 7 in the B/C/S version. Oh, we were already on that page. My apologies. Yes. And in the English version, can you scroll down to the bottom of that page. Yes. Thank you very much. Now, you see that here there are -- there's a section of this record which includes proposals made by Dr. Simonovic, and under number 2 he proposes that the agreement on the neutralisation of the hospital -- so he states that it was indeed signed by General Raseta and Hebrang, and he proposes to call for a hearing Major Sljivancanin, Dr. Bosanac, and Colonel Vojnovic. Now, first of all we have heard about Major Sljivancanin and we have heard about Dr. Bosanac. Are you aware of who Colonel Vojnovic was?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the man personally, but I believe that this Colonel Vojnovic was supposed to take over the hospital on behalf of the Military Medical Academy. When that meeting was organised on the 20th, I believe I heard from Dr. Njavro that the man's name was Colonel Vojnovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, was there ever a hearing which included both Major Sljivancanin and yourself?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this document, please, it's 65 ter 6402?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 6402 will be Exhibit P1473.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, you did mention to us earlier that you took part in some of these meetings. When was the first time that you took part in a meeting of this commission?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first participated in one in the summer. I believe it was the 6th of June, 1992, because I saw these reports, and I saw that the last item concerned the wounded from Vukovar who could not be identified. Nobody could tell what became of them. It was a time when I was heavily involved in attempts to find out what had happened to the wounded. I looked everywhere, and I insisted with Professor Hebrang and Mr. Kostic, who was a member of the delegation to Geneva, that they include me in these negotiations. So on these two occasions I participated. I suggested that experts be brought before that commission, this Dr. Stankovic who performed identifications, as well as Dr. Strinovic, so that they provide a report on the identification of the dead. I also proposed that the commission hear as witnesses people who had been on those buses from the hospital, Emil Cakalic and Stjepan Guncevic, that they should also attend a session of that commission in Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Doctor, it is correct that records or minutes of these meetings are also available?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, throughout this time after your release and in early 1992, what information was available in relation to the fate of the patients and the staff from the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the ICRC and services involved in searches were not providing any answers about any of the persons who had been taken away from the Vukovar Hospital and were still missing, and I know this from personal experience because we were looking for my father-in-law, I had a very strong suspicion that they were no longer alive. And those witnesses who had been released as part of an exchange, Emil Cakalic and Stjepan Guncevic, told me that they had seen my father-in-law in that hangar at Ovcara along with some other people I knew, but they were not on any ICRC lists or any other lists of other services involved in the search for missing persons, and we never got any confirmation from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when did Emil Cakalic and Stjepan Guncevic provide this information to you, at what point in time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After they were released from prison. I see it's written Stjepan Guncevic here. After spending time in that hangar in Ovcara, they were taken back to Velepromet or perhaps Moditeks or one of those collection centres, and after that they spent time in prisons in Serbia and they were released. After they were released, I discussed it with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I see the date or the month. Are you able to help us with when approximately this was that they were released from prison?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was in May 1992, but I believe there is precise

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, were you able to have access to the Vukovar area after your release from prison?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went back to Vukovar for the first time in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And what information, if any, did you have during 1992 in relation to what was occurring in Vukovar itself after your release from Sremska Mitrovica?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, we had information from people who were coming out of Vukovar either via Hungary or had been released as part of exchanges with prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And with regards to early 1992, did you receive any information as to what was happening in Vukovar town itself?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out that a Serbian government was established in Vukovar, that everybody who stayed behind was subjected to torture, many Croats were driven out, and I remember in particular one journalist who was in a sort of work camp where they were made to bury the dead. Also, the husband of a nurse came. He was part of a group that was burying the dead, and he brought some lists. We received some information from people who belatedly came out of Vukovar. An elderly woman who was the mother-in-law of one of our nurses came to see me and said that she also had her husband taken away, that he was killed, her child was taken to Serbia. We had all sorts of information about the torture people were subjected to in that period in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And, Doctor, you explained to us a little earlier that you continued sending appeals following your release. Can you look at the next document which is 65 ter 5902 at tab 108, please. No, I'm sorry. This is the I don't think document. Could you please take it down. Just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: My mistake, Your Honours. This is actually 65 ter 1037, at tab 52.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It's dated the 22nd of April, so clearly after your release. Can you tell us the circumstances surrounding the sending of this appeal?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's something I sent after those two women had come to see me, saying how that nurse and that man, her husband, were killed. They wanted me to do something if I could to try to protect the people who had stayed there, and that's how I came to sign this appeal.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Who did you send it to?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an office in Zagreb at that time, a UN field office, dealing with humanitarian issues, covering UNHCR and UNCRO. We sent it to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 1037 will be Exhibit P1474.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, this concludes my examination-in-chief at this time. As announced earlier, depending on developments this afternoon, we may decide to re-open our examination-in-chief tomorrow in relation to the DVD that Dr. Bosanac provided us over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic here, and I'm going to ask you a few questions. I'm afraid we're going to run over into tomorrow. If any of my questions are not clear or you wish to have further clarification, feel free to ask me and I'll do my best. Did you understand that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to start at the outset by asking you some questions about the evacuation of patients and civilians from the hospital on the 19th and the 20th of November, and to start with that, I'd like you to take a look again at the evacuation agreement. Could we have P1461, please, which is Prosecution tab 35. Now, ma'am, you've already testified about this document that's coming up in front of you. Do you remember when you first saw this document as such?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it as such for the first time after I was released from prison. I did not see it back in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is my understanding correct that it was Dr. Hebrang who was giving you information about the content of this agreement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I'd just like to focus your attention on a few matters that were not addressed by the Prosecution, and if we look at paragraph 1, it indicates the various parties to the agreement. Did Dr. Hebrang, as you can recall, specifically inform you that it was the JNA that was a party to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He told me that General Raseta was representing the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says there at paragraph 2: "The Republic of Croatia and the YPA undertook to guarantee a cease-fire in the area of Vukovar Hospital and along the agreed evacuation route." Now, let me just pause there. Did Dr. Hebrang inform you that the cease-fire was supposed to cover not only the hospital but also the entirety of the evacuation route?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not tell me that in precisely those terms, but he said that agreement had been signed and the shooting would stop, the attacks would stop, and that the evacuation would begin under the auspices of the ICRC and the European Monitoring Mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, did he inform you in general terms that the parties were responsible for ensuring the security of the evacuation convoys?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And paragraph 2 goes on: "This guarantee would cover both regular forces and irregular units in the areas in which they would respectively have responsibility for the evacuation operation." Now, thinking back to the time, and I know that it's a long time ago, but do you remember whether Dr. Hebrang informed you that this agreement covered not only the JNA as such, but it also covered all what are described here as irregular units that might be associated with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not explain to me so precisely every article of this agreement. He only said that the hospital would be neutralised, and he asked me how many medical and other vehicles needed to be prepared for the evacuation and that everything would be organised by the ICRC and the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And looking down at paragraph 4 of this agreement, it says: "The YPA will provide suitable military vehicles for the movement from Vukovar to Zidine." Was it your understanding that the patients would be physically transported in JNA vehicles?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was my understanding. As for the route, Vukovar Prilevci, Bogdanovci and Luzac pertained to in item 3 as the one to be taken and I also understood that they were to be transferred by vehicles to Nustar where they were supposed to be moved to the ambulances and buses provided by the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm finished with that document; it can be removed from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Bosanac, as I understand from your testimony earlier today, you ventured out of the hospital on the morning of the 19th of November, and you talked toward a railroad bridge. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then when you arrived at the railroad bridge you saw what you described as reservists as well as different members of paramilitary forces. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did these paramilitary forces include individuals wearing long beards?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a military truck full of different soldiers. Some had military uniform, olive-drab uniforms. There were people in civilian clothes. They differed. I didn't recognise anyone. When those people saw us approaching, since I wasn't going alone, Marin Bilic [as interpreted] was with me and Senka Vuko who was a medical radiologist and acting as interpreter on that occasion since we expected to encounter ICRC representatives there, when they saw us, given the fact that she and I were in our white medical coats, they called one of their superiors, telling them that we appeared there. One of them who was in an olive-drab uniform and a helmet resembling --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause there so I can take this in pieces because you're giving a lot of information, and I'd like to focus if I can on a few specific points. Are you all right, Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you okay to continue?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You said that these various -- these different soldiers were in a truck. Were they in a truck together, all these different soldiers in a truck together?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And -- and was that a JNA truck?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you said that they called one of their superiors. Could you describe the superior?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was an olive-drab uniform and he wore a helmet like one of those we saw in the footage. I saw several such trucks on the road called Priljevo that could be seen from the railroad bridge. I saw quite a few people getting onto those trucks as ordered by those soldiers. The superior officer or soldier asked who we were. I said we came from the hospital and that we were looking for the ICRC. He said that there was no ICRC there. I asked him if he could use a phone to call someone who could provide us with information as to the whereabouts of the ICRC; he said he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Doctor, could you ask you to pause there. This superior, was he wearing a JNA uniform?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you remember his rank?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 1D252, please, which is Defence tab 29, and if we could have page 28 of this document. This is an interlinear transcription, or it's a transcription which contains both the B/C/S and the English on the same pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Bosanac, this is a portion of a statement that you behave in 1993 to a Canadian investigator who, as I understand it, was acting on behalf of the ECMM. Do you remember having given a statement like that in 1993 to a Canadian investigator? Let me correct myself. Let me --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably did. I can't recall. I don't remember. I do remember providing certain statements at the school of medicine in their department of information, but I don't know what the purpose of it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, here's what's recorded in this interview, this transcript of your interview which was taken about two years after the events, and you're describing this particular encounter and you say: "A captain appeared. They addressed him as captain." Does that refresh your memory that it was a JNA captain who was the superior?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I really don't remember. Probably. When I gave this statement in 1993, perhaps my recollection was better. I do remember, though, that it was a soldier or an officer belonging to the JNA who told us then that there was no ICRC there and that we should return to the hospital. He said he couldn't reach them because his job was evacuation only up to the bridge, and beyond the bridge, which was the area where the hospital was, was not within his responsibility according to his words. That's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you understand that this captain was acting as the superior for all of these soldiers who you saw in the truck?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you see any bearded soldiers - and when I say "bearded," I mean paramilitary soldiers with long beards - did you see any such individuals sitting on JNA APCs?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean at that moment when I was at the bridge or otherwise?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: On that occasion.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that I saw bearded men on that occasion, but I could see that they were all unkempt and unshaved, but I did see these true paramilitaries with beards and knives. They were also in JNA vehicles. One such person actually went along with us en route to Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you were -- when you were taken to Negoslavci by the JNA officer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You're saying that one of these long-bearded paramilitary soldiers accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, after this incident at the railway bridge, as I understand it you returned to the hospital and you waited there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then at around 12.00 or 12.30, a military vehicle arrived carrying JNA soldiers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you spoke to someone who presented himself as the commander of these JNA soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And on that occasion you asked him to post someone at the entrance to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did he tell you that he was going to post a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you see the military policeman?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an olive-drab uniform, but they had white leather belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And amongst that -- amongst the soldiers who arrived on that occasion, which you've said is around 12.00 or 12.30 in front of the hospital, how many of them were dressed as such with white belts?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, say four or five.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many soldiers in total there were who arrived there at that occasion?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 15, although I don't remember exactly. I do know that immediately after the jeep with the commander arrived, I talked to him and then returned to the hospital to tell my colleagues, the doctors, that I was to go to Negoslavci and then I left. I don't know how many arrived and how many there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then you went and had this conversation with Colonel Mrksic in Negoslavci. I won't ask you to go over that entire episode in detail, but I do have one or two points of clarification to ask you. Was it your impression when you arrived and started speaking to Colonel Mrksic about the need to evacuate patients from the hospital that this was the first he had heard of it, or was it your impression that Colonel Mrksic was already informed that an agreement had been reached for the evacuation of patients?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he had been informed. I think he had been, because he told me that if we insisted on the route Bogdanovci-Marinci-Nustar he had to de-mine the area of Zidine. At that moment I didn't know what Zidine was. He said it was their military training ground and that he would have to de-mine a part of it. That's how I knew he must have been aware of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And was it your impression that Colonel Mrksic considered himself responsible for carrying out the evacuation of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is that in fact consistent with everything that you had heard from General Raseta about how the evacuation was to be carried out, that it was to be carried out under the supervision and control of Colonel Mrksic?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, as I understand it, you then returned to the hospital, and am I right that you arrived at the hospital around 3.00 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were the military policemen still guarding the entrance to the hospital when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: How many did you see performing that function, guarding the entrance to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were they armed?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were they allowing anyone to enter the hospital?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who so wished, such as Bogdan Kuzmic and many others who walked throughout the hospital. I recall an incident in the evening. It was on the 19th in the evening. Marko Mandic came to tell me that there was some ruckus at the entrance. I came out, and I could see some men in military uniform trying to enter the hospital, but the military policemen wouldn't let them through. There was a lot of noise. As it turned out, some members of the so-called White Eagles wanted to enter, including the son of a doctor of ours. When I came outside, the doctor came out of the out-patient clinic, and he told me -- he told them that they could let his son through, and he told me to go back to my office and that he was to take care of hospital safety. I recall that incident, recalling that they didn't let in just anyone. It was on the 19th in the evening before I was taken to Negoslavci for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what time, if you can recall, was it that you saw Major Sljivancanin in the hospital for the first time?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him for the first time in the afternoon, around 4.00 or 5.00 p.m., by which time I had returned from Negoslavci.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you testified earlier today that he said that from that moment on, I quote: "He was in charge of the hospital and he had to evacuate civilians first."

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did he tell you on that occasion that he was evacuating civilians to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He just said that he had to evacuate civilians. I heard that it was actually taking place from Zeljka Zgonjanin who was on the first floor making a list of civilians. She told me that they were taking out men and taking them away while they left the women behind. In other words, they were separating men from women, and I came out into the yard to see what was going on. It was then that I encountered Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have page 46 of the document that's on the screen, please. And again, Dr. Bosanac, this is your interview in 1993, and I want to see if this will refresh your -- your memory about whether Mr. -- Major Sljivancanin told you that he was taking these civilians to Velepromet. And if we could scroll down the page. And I'm just going to read the English, but of course you can follow along in the B/C/S. "Zeljka came to me in the office to come because there was panic there. I went there and saw that they were going down out of the main entrance to the new hospital. The army was taking them in trucks which were lined up along the side of Gunduliceva Street." Now, let's just stop there. Is it true that the civilians were being loaded beyond trucks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were those JNA military trucks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then you go on: "They first took away the men, and that was why there was a commotion, because the women were crying and shouting, and that is when I first saw Sljivancanin. 'What are you doing? Why are you taking these people?' He said they were going to Velepromet, and he was constantly telling these people, 'You will be able to go wherever you want. The Yugoslav federal army has liberated you. These men are only going to have their names taken. You will meet again at Velepromet.'" Now, having read that, Dr. Bosanac, does that refresh your memory that Major Sljivancanin expressly told you that he was taking those people to Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I know I heard for the first time of Velepromet when I met my mother en route back from Negoslavci. She told me that my in-laws were taken to Velepromet. So probably it was the case, although I don't recall it precisely. He did say that they were being taken there to be registered, but it was a farce, because many of them were killed at Velepromet too. The fact is that the ICRC was not in charge of evacuation, neither the evacuation of the hospital or of civilians. The ECMM was not in charge either. It was all done -- it was all arranged by Major Sljivancanin, the JNA, and the paramilitary troops that were alongside them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And let me pick up on that last item, the paramilitary troops. Do you remember on this occasion when you saw civilians being taken out of the hospital on the afternoon of the 19th of November? Did you -- under the supervision of Major Sljivancanin, did you see paramilitary troops participating in that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the civilians were being taken away and put on the trucks? No. They were reservists like Bogdan Kuzmic and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, whether they were paramilitary or something else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 0247 -- excuse me. Let me repeat that number. 65 ter 02742, which is Defence tab 11. And this would be paragraph 82 in both the English and the B/C/S. Now, we're looking for paragraph 82 in the B/C/S. Now, Dr. Bosanac, this is what you said in your statement that was prepared for your testimony in the Seselj case, and you signed this, and this -- in this paragraph, what you say is: "She," and you're referring to Zeljka Zgonjanin, "she told me she did not know what to do because there was --"

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just one moment. Can you check whether it is on the screen, because I don't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we adjust the position of the B/C/S? It's slightly cut off. It's a question of the margins being cut off. I can't see the left side of the document, and I'm sure that Dr. Bosanac can't either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which item is that? Which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could just very slightly move the left document a little bit towards the left. Yes. That would be perfect. We're getting there. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, it should be the very top paragraph on the screen in front of you. And what you say there is --

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 82, is that what you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, the very top paragraph on the screen.

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "She told me she did not know what to do because there was panic upstairs since JNA soldiers were separating the men from their families. Vidic went up with her to see what was happening, and I got out and saw the JNA which was in charge of the operation. Apart from them, I saw the Territorial Defence members amongst them, also the Chetniks who were nervously walking around looking to recognise Croatian soldiers, and I cannot assume what their intentions were." Dr. Bosanac, does that refresh your memory that not only did you see JNA soldiers separating men and removing them from the hospital, but that also there were, as you described them, TO members and, as you say here, Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I can't read everything because it's too small. I can't make out everything that's in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, can you read the portion I've read, and do you agree that that's what's there?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read the following: "Vidic went upstairs to see what was happening, and I got up and saw the JNA which was in charge of the operation. Apart from them, I saw Territorial Defence members among them, also Chetniks who were nervously walking around looking to recognise Croatian soldiers, and I cannot assume what their intentions were." I can read that. I can't recall exactly when I provided this statement. I suppose I --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, what's actually most important, and I'm sorry to interrupt you, what's most important is as you sit there now, can you remember on that day, on the 19th of November, can you remember that you saw not only JNA soldiers separating civilians from their families, you also saw what you describe here as Chetniks and TO members?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat that I saw members of the TO and of paramilitary forces. One such man drove a road in the same car with us. I can't recall whether I saw them by the truck when people were being --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Dr. Bosanac, I'm terribly sorry to interrupt again, but I'm just talking now about in the hospital on the afternoon of the 19th when the civilians are being removed. Did you see Chetniks doing that?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't see them being taken away by Chetniks. I did see them being directed to the trucks by the soldiers, and I also saw TO members. They were not young soldiers, conscripts, but reservists such as Bogdan Kuzmic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this entire operation was being directed by Major Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this wasn't a question of Major Sljivancanin just allowing this to happen. This was something that was being actively ordered and directed by Major Sljivancanin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present there non-stop. I said what he told me when I asked about it. Major Sljivancanin was very arrogant at the time. He told me that it was none of my business, that he was in charge, and that he was going to implement it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And by saying that he was in charge, wouldn't you infer that that meant that he was responsible for removing those civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And he was very resentful of what he perceived to be your invention in the matter, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: VESNA BOSANAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I see the clock, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Dr. Bosanac, this is the end of today's hearing. We will continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. I remind you that you're still under oath, which means that you cannot discuss your testimony with anybody, nor can you talk to any of the parties. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of April, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.01 p.m.,
